examples.en: What color do you like?
Does this come in another color?
The color is different from the photo, so I want to exchange it.
The child is coloring in the picture.
I like brightly colored clothes.

explain: “색깔”이라고도 해요. “무슨 색깔을 좋아해요?”도 맞아요. 색 이름 뒤에는 보통 “색”만 붙여요: 빨간색, 파란색.
explain_en: You can also say 색깔, so “무슨 색깔을 좋아해요?” is fine too. After a color name, people usually add just 색: 빨간색, 파란색.

dis.h: color; short, basic, used in compounds

p.n: Same meaning. 색 is shorter and also forms words like 빨간색; 색깔 is the fuller everyday word.

examples.en: I'm going to buy a black bag.
My younger sibling has jet-black hair.
The night sky is dark, so you can see the stars well.
My face got deeply tanned at the beach in summer.
A black cat is on the chair.

explain: “까맣게 잊다”처럼 ‘완전히’라는 뜻으로도 써요. 약속을 하나도 기억하지 못할 때 “까맣게 잊었어요”라고 해요.

phrases.example: 시험 결과를 기다리느라 속이 까맣게 탔어요.
phrases.nuance_en: used when you are very worried and anxious inside

explain: “검은색”은 “까만색”과 같은 색이에요. 한국에서는 장례식에 보통 검은색 옷을 입고 가요.

explain_en: 검은색 and 까만색 name the same color. In Korea people usually wear black clothes to a funeral.

dis.h: standard everyday word for black color

p.n: Almost the same; 검정색 is a noun-based variant.

examples.en: I bought white sneakers.
It snowed, so the streets are all white.
I hung a picture on the white wall.

examples.ko: 하얀 강아지가 우리 집 앞에 있어요.
examples.en: A white puppy is in front of our house.

examples.ko: 병원 방은 벽도 침대도 다 하얘요.
examples.en: In the hospital room, even the walls and the bed are all white.

explain: “좋다”는 “좋아요”인데 “하얗다”는 “하얘요”예요. ㅎ이 사라지고 모양이 바뀌는 ㅎ 불규칙이에요. “하얬어요”도 같고, “하얀”은 ㅎ만 없어져요.

phrases.en_equiv: to turn pale (from fear or shock)

phrases.en_equiv: to stay up all night without sleeping

explain_en: 빨갛다 is a ㅎ-irregular adjective, so it becomes 빨개요 and 빨간. In writing you also see 붉다, as in 붉은 노을 (a red sunset).

p.n: 붉다 is possible but sounds more literary; 빨갛다 is the natural everyday choice.

explain: 빨간색은 한국 축구 응원의 색이기도 해요. 이름을 빨간색으로 쓰는 것을 피하는 사람도 있어서, 이름은 보통 파란색이나 검은색으로 써요.

p.n: Almost the same; 빨강 is the plain noun form without 색.

examples.ko: 우리 반에서 제 키가 제일 커요.
examples.en: I'm the tallest in our class.

explain_en: For height, Koreans say 크다/작다 (big/small), never 높다 (high). In Korea people talk about height quite openly, even with someone they just met.

p.n: 키 is for people and plants; 높이 fits any object.

examples.en: My younger sibling is tall and slim.
My older sister works out a lot, so she's slim.
This laptop is slim and light.

examples.ko: 이 병은 날씬해서 한 손으로 잡기 쉬워요.
examples.en: This bottle is slim, so it is easy to hold with one hand.

examples.ko: 이 우산은 날씬해서 작은 가방에도 들어가요.
examples.en: This umbrella is slim, so it fits in a small bag too.

explain: “날씬하다”는 사람에게도 쓰지만, 노트북·휴대폰·병처럼 모양이 얇고 깔끔한 물건에도 자주 써요.

explain_en: 날씬하다 is used for people, but it is also common for slim, neat-looking things such as laptops, phones and bottles.

examples.en: Our cat is a little chubby.
I was a bit chubby as a kid.
My friend is chubby, but he runs fast.

examples.ko: 고양이가 뚱뚱해요? — 네, 너무 뚱뚱해서 못 뛰어요.

What's the new employee like? — He's very handsome.
A good-looking actor is in the drama.

explain: “잘생겼어요”는 지금 모습이어도 과거형으로 말해요. “잘생긴 사람”처럼 써요. 보통 남자에게 많이 쓰고, 여자에게는 “예뻐요”를 써요.

explain_en: Even for how someone looks now, Korean uses the past form: 잘생겼어요, 잘생긴 사람. It is mostly said about men; for women, 예뻐요 is the usual word.
